newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs end sharply lower due to rate rise concerns.
newsitem.headline: JGBs end sharply lower due to rate rise concerns.

text.p: The key June 10-year Japanese government bond futures contract ended sharply down on Friday, after falling to a seven-month low earlier in the day, due to massive selling triggered by fears of higher interest rates.
Traders said all types of participants began unloading their JGB holdings this morning.
"The market started to factor in a scenario where Japan may raise interest rates in July," said a dealer at a long-term credit bank's securities unit.
The June ended at 123.45, down sharply from the previous day's close of 124.05. Turnover was 78.885 contracts.
Sentiment in the JGB market was dampened after remarks late Thursday by a senior Finance Ministry official aimed at curbing strength in the dollar, which fuelled fears of higher Japanese rates.
"Japanese authorities' efforts to keep the yen from falling can be interpreted as both a bullish and a bearish factor," said a dealer at a city bank's securities unit.
"But this time, they fuelled fears of higher interest rates. If verbal and actual market intervention do not work, Japan may raise interest rates to keep the yen from falling further," he said.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said on Thursday that a strengthening of the yen to 103 yen to the dollar is possible when looking at currency fluctuations over the past year.
JGBs were lifted off their lows in afternoon trade due to buy-backs and investor buying of cash JGBs, traders said.

"Scattered buying of the key 182nd JGB and the 190th to 194th JGBs was seen. Regional investors and agricultural financial institutions seemed to be behind the buying," a trader for a brokerage house said.

The premium for the June JGB futures put options with a strike price of 123.00 rose as high as 1.00 on Friday, and foreigners were detected selling their holdings for profits, the brokerage house trader said.
Foreigners sold the put options for profits while domestic investors bought for hedging purposes, the trader said.

The Industrial Bank of Japan's 1.60 percent five-year bank debenture issued in April was traded at 2.27 percent on Friday morning. Based on this yield, traders said IBJ's May long-term prime rate, which will be announced on Monday, may be raised by 0.6 or 0.7 percentage point from 2.5 percent in April.
